notes.title: Retail exchange and return workflow caution
notes.body: In one retail-support transcript, the agent authenticated via name+ZIP, found an order without the customer having its number, checked product variants, and obtained explicit confirmation before submitting a return. It warned that an order's exchange/modify action is one-time and later correctly did not submit the tentative lamp exchange when the customer declined; the customer instead confirmed a water-bottle return, which the tool recorded as 'return requested.' Lesson/caution: for delivered-order exchanges, gather every intended item before the one-time action and explain its consequence, but distinguish an unsubmitted exchange from a completed one; if the customer changes course, confirm the exact return item and refund method before acting. This reflects the provided policy and this transcript; no separate evaluation feedback or grading details were provided.

notes.title: Retail delivered return/exchange workflow observations
notes.body: From one retail support transcript (no separate evaluation feedback; do not treat prior behavior as necessarily correct): authenticate first via email or name+ZIP, then use account/order records to identify the order and matching item IDs. For delivered-order return/exchange, verify status and product variant availability/prices from tools; distinguish product ID from item ID. For exchanges, collect all intended items and replacement variants before the one-per-order exchange call, identify any price difference and valid payment method, state action details, and obtain explicit confirmation before mutation. Transcript warned that submitting an exchange uses a one-time per-order exchange action; the exchange was never submitted, so that warning was not tested. The transcript additionally claimed no later exchange could be done for the order; do not generalize beyond the one-time exchange constraint without verifying policy/tool behavior. When user instead requests a return, check exact item and status, use original payment method or existing gift card, state order/items/refund destination and obtain explicit confirmation; after tool success report the resulting status and email instructions. In the observed case, the water bottle-only return was confirmed and tool returned status 'return requested'; no exchange was performed. Stop before any database-changing tool call until confirmation is explicit.

notes.title: Retail exchange workflow observations
notes.body: For retail exchange work under the provided policy: authenticate first via email or name+ZIP, then verify order ownership/status and item IDs; fetch product variants and use item IDs (not product IDs) to confirm same-product, available replacements matching the user's stated constraints. Present exact old/new items and price difference/payment method, mention return process, and stop for explicit confirmation before any update; after the call, report only what the tool confirms. When multiple variants satisfy a request, avoid implying the presented subset is exhaustive unless all qualifying options were checked/presented.

notes.title: Retail returns: payment-method limits and escalation
notes.body: In a retail-support experience, an authenticated customer's delivered order was paid by Visa, and they requested a return refund to PayPal. The provided policy allowed refunds only to the original payment method or an existing gift card. The customer explicitly requested a human agent after rejecting the eligible original-card option; the assistant transferred with a concise summary and then issued the required transfer message. No evaluation feedback was provided, so this should not be treated as independently verified correct/incorrect. Lesson/caution: for delivered returns, do not promise or route a refund to a different payment type; clarify eligible destinations, and escalate when the customer explicitly requests a human because the desired arrangement cannot be completed within the policy. Before submitting any return, obtain explicit confirmation of the return details.

notes.title: Retail returns: authenticate, verify eligibility, confirm, escalate when needed
notes.body: In a retail support interaction, authenticate first (email or name + ZIP), then use account order records to identify relevant orders and verify status/payment details before promising an action. For delivered returns, collect exact order and item list plus refund method; only original payment method or an existing gift card is allowed. If requested method is unsupported, explain constraint and offer valid option; do not submit return without explicit confirmation of the order, items, and eligible refund method. If the customer explicitly asks for a human because the issue cannot be handled within policy, transfer via the handoff tool, then send the required transfer notice. In the reviewed case, no return was submitted; customer insisted on PayPal although the order was paid by Visa, requested a human, and transfer succeeded. No separate evaluation feedback was provided.

notes.title: Retail pending-order address update workflow
notes.body: For similar retail support tasks under the supplied policy: (1) Authenticate first via account email or name + ZIP, even if user supplies an ID; keep to one customer. (2) Look up the specified order and verify it belongs to the authenticated user and is pending before modifying. (3) State the current address and exact proposed change, preserving all unchanged address fields, and obtain explicit yes confirmation before any database update. (4) After confirmation, make only the requested update; use one tool call at a time. (5) Inspect the tool result for the changed address and status, then report the outcome without claiming more than it verifies. In the observed case these steps were followed: identity lookup by name/ZIP, order lookup showed pending and Suite 640, confirmation obtained for Suite 641 only, update tool returned Suite 641 and pending. No separate evaluation feedback was provided; this describes observed behavior, not an assertion of grading or correctness.

notes.title: Retail requests combining return and exchange on one delivered order
notes.body: In a retail-agent experience, a customer explicitly authorized returning two items and exchanging another item on the same delivered order. The return tool succeeded first and changed the order status to “return requested”; a human-transfer summary then stated the exchange tool requires delivered status, so the exchange could not be submitted. The transfer succeeded; no exchange completion is evidenced. Lesson/caution: when a customer requests both a return and an exchange on one order, inspect tool/status constraints before submitting either action. If one action changes status such that the other may become unavailable, do not assume both can be completed sequentially or choose an order arbitrarily; clarify/escalate before committing the first action. This is an observed failure mode in this experience, not proof of all implementations’ behavior.

notes.title: Retail pending-order service procedure
notes.body: For similar retail support work under the supplied policy: authenticate first via account email, or if lookup fails, request first/last name plus ZIP; retain uncertainty and do not treat failed lookup as authentication. After identifying the user, retrieve order details and verify ownership/status before discussing or acting. For payment requests, state that only one payment method can be used (no split); inspect profile for an eligible different method before saying none is available. For item-level cancellation requests, do not promise partial cancellation; pending-order cancellation is whole-order only. For variant-price checks, fetch details for each product, compare only available variants, keep each replacement within the same product type, sum the selected prices, and state whether the target is met. Item modification can only be done once and blocks later modification/cancellation, so collect all changes and payment method, explain consequences, list exact details, and obtain explicit yes before action; if user declines, make no changes. For pending cancellation, verify pending status, obtain one of the permitted reasons ('no longer needed' or 'ordered by mistake'), state order/reason/refund amount and destination/timing, and get explicit yes before cancel tool; then report tool-confirmed result. In the observed interaction, five cheapest available variants summed correctly to $1,130.85 (above $950); no modification was made. For similar retail exchange requests, follow this ordered procedure, based on one past conversation (not proof that every tool/policy implementation behaves identically):
1. Authenticate first via account email or name + ZIP; only then inspect the user's orders.
2. Identify the exact order and item ID, confirm delivered status, and retrieve product details. Distinguish product ID from item ID; only offer an available variant of the same product, preserving requested options where possible. Do not prematurely state a type-of-vacuum/category restriction when the actual rule is same product/variant options.
3. Calculate and clearly state the price difference, payment/refund destination, and exact old/new item IDs. Since exchange is once per order, explicitly ask the user to confirm this is the complete list of items to exchange.
4. Obtain explicit confirmation of the exchange and an acceptable payment method before calling an update tool. A user's confirmation of item selection alone does not authorize proceeding if the payment path remains unresolved.
5. If user requests a gift-card difference/refund, check available profile payment methods and applicable policy/tool capability. Do not claim a gift card can be issued or use an unlisted card. If the desired option cannot be handled through available actions, explain the limitation and transfer to a human agent; do not execute exchange before resolving payment.
6. After any transfer tool succeeds, send the prescribed transfer notice. In the observed case transfer succeeded; no exchange was submitted, and the feedback supplied no evaluation detail.

notes.title: Retail exchanges: verify scope, match variants, confirm before action
notes.body:
In one retail-support exchange, the agent authenticated by name+ZIP, inspected the customer’s orders to identify the delivered order, inspected product variants and availability, then presented the exchange item, cheapest available replacement meeting the requested water-resistance level, price difference/refund method, and requested explicit confirmation including whether all exchange items were listed. After the customer confirmed, the exchange tool returned status “exchange requested,” and the agent reported the refund amount/method and return-instructions email. This sequence appeared to complete successfully; no evaluation feedback was provided, so correctness is not independently verified.

For similar work: (1) authenticate via email or name+ZIP before account actions; stop if identity cannot be verified. (2) Locate the relevant order and check status; exchanges require delivered status. (3) Confirm target item and inspect its product variants; preserve product type, match requested options/constraints, and select only an available replacement. If “cheapest from the rest of the same order” could mean an already-purchased unit rather than a cheapest available catalog variant, clarify before proceeding. (4) Calculate/report price difference and an allowed payment/refund method; verify any applicable gift-card balance requirement. (5) State the exact order, old/new item IDs, financial difference/method, and ask explicit yes-confirmation plus confirmation that all exchange items are included; stop until received. (6) Call the exchange action once only, then report the tool’s actual status and next steps without promising beyond its result.

notes.title: Retail workflow caution: confirm every return before action
notes.body: In one retail-support interaction, the assistant authenticated via one of two candidate emails after the first lookup failed, then mistakenly submitted return requests for all items in two delivered orders before receiving the customer's required explicit confirmation of order, items, and refund payment method. Customer objected; assistant acknowledged the mistake, explained it could not undo/change the requests with available tools, and escalated to a human. The customer had said they needed cash, but recorded original payment for these orders was a gift card; no actual-payment alternative was visible in the profile/order data. Later, after explicit confirmation of both pending order IDs and allowed reason, assistant cancelled them; refunds were immediately returned to the gift card. Lesson: do not treat a broad request such as “cancel or return everything” as confirmation to perform all returns; first list each delivered-order return, selected item IDs, and eligible refund method, then obtain explicit yes. Clearly distinguish a requested return from a completed refund, and do not promise cash or redirection when unavailable. Applicable to retail workflows governed by explicit pre-action confirmation; escalation is appropriate when the requested remedy is outside available tools. No separate grading feedback was provided.

notes.title: Retail order exchange/return guidance from bookshelf-to-camera case
notes.body: In a retail-agent conversation, customer authenticated via name + ZIP, then profile/order lookup established a bookshelf order was status `processed` with tracking ID. The agent appropriately treated `processed` as not eligible for return/exchange (actions are limited to pending/delivered as applicable), and did not claim tracking proved shipment: suggested checking carrier, while noting shipment wasn't explicit in order details. Policy limits exchanges to a different variant of the same product type, so bookshelf→camera is not an exchange regardless of price; returning first does not make it an exchange. A separate camera purchase is distinct from return/exchange. For similar requests: (1) authenticate first by email or name+ZIP even if user supplies an ID; (2) retrieve order and check status/items; (3) explain scope: pending orders may be modified, delivered orders may be returned/exchanged, processed orders are not eligible for those actions; do not equate processed+tracking with confirmed shipped; (4) for exchange, verify same product type and different available variant, and explain price-difference/payment requirements if applicable; (5) if cross-type change, explain no direct exchange and only discuss a separate purchase if useful; (6) for return, wait until status is delivered, identify item(s), require refund method (original payment method or existing gift card), and obtain explicit confirmation of order/items/action before database update. Stop if status or eligibility fails; don't initiate action. In the case, assistant said eligible payment method without specifying the policy's exact refund choices, so future answers should state the restriction. No separate evaluation feedback was provided; no grading details inferred.

notes.title: Retail order modifications: variant checks and mismatches
notes.body: For retail pending-order workflows, authenticate first via email or name+ZIP, retrieve order and product variants, and confirm status plus exact available item IDs/options before changing anything. Before database updates, present all intended changes and get explicit yes; for one-time item modifications, collect every requested item and disclose irreversibility. The user must specify the payment method for any price difference; do not choose a stored method merely because it was used originally. In one public experience, product lookup showed backpack item 5917587651 as grey/medium/polyester, while after confirmed modification the tool response unexpectedly labeled that item as black/low/USB (matching the lamp) and reported an unexpected $14.06 gift-card charge. Assistant correctly stopped further edits and transferred for human review rather than asserting the change succeeded or trying another one-time modification. Preserve uncertainty: the anomalous response could reflect a tool/system mismatch; actual fulfillment state was not independently verified. Address update response did confirm the new address. Procedure: (1) authenticate and retrieve order; stop if identity/order ownership cannot be established. (2) Check pending status and variant availability/details. (3) Explain any unavailable exact combination and alternatives, delta/payment implications, and one-time restriction; ask user to select and explicitly confirm all changes and payment method. (4) Execute only supported confirmed actions, then inspect returned state against each requested item ID, name, and options. (5) If output conflicts or payment is unexpected, do not claim success or retry an irreversible action; confirm only fields actually supported by tool response, explain discrepancy, and escalate if it cannot be resolved within available tools.

User requested address change to their default Charlotte address, backpack grey/medium/polyester, and lamp black while preserving low brightness (tool variants showed black low-brightness USB available, so disclosed power-source change). User explicitly confirmed all changes. Address update tool returned the requested address. Item-modification call used the correct apparent mapping of new item IDs (backpack 5917587651; lamp 9190635437) and gift card; its response unexpectedly listed both the Backpack and Desk Lamp with the same black/low/USB options and price $153.23, despite product lookup showing backpack 5917587651 as grey/medium/polyester/laptop at $212.79 and lamp 9190635437 as black/low/USB at $153.23. Response also recorded a $14.06 gift-card charge and indicated one-time modification used, preventing further item changes/cancellation. Assistant disclosed mismatch, confirmed address, and transferred to a human after user asked for correction and whether charge could be shifted/refunded to PayPal. Transfer succeeded; no human resolution or payment-method remedy is recorded. Treat the tool response as anomalous/unverified, not as proof of actual fulfillment state. Evaluation feedback supplied: none.

notes.title: Retail order modification: confirm difference-payment method and verify returned item mapping
notes.body: In a retail support interaction, user authenticated via name+ZIP; pending order items/address and variants were checked. User explicitly confirmed address change and two desired item changes. Address update succeeded. For item modification, the tool call mapped item IDs in the intended order (backpack -> 5917587651, lamp -> 9190635437), but the returned order details showed both item lines with black/low/USB options, an apparent backend/result mismatch. The modification was one-time and further edits unavailable, so assistant transferred to a human after reporting the mismatch and gift card charge; transfer completion is verified, subsequent correction/refund outcome is unknown. Lesson/caution: before an irreversible one-time item modification, verify each selected item ID against the correct product and options, and explicitly establish the payment method for any price difference rather than assuming the original gift card. After a tool returns inconsistent product/variant mapping, do not claim correction; preserve the discrepancy and escalate when no supported corrective action exists. No separate evaluation feedback was provided.

notes.title: Retail pending item modification: distinguish refund tender from payment change
notes.body: In a retail-support interaction, user requested cancellation of a pending five-item order and a change to an i9 laptop, asking to switch its payment method from PayPal to Visa. The agent authenticated via name+ZIP, identified orders, got cancellation confirmation (including accepted reason), and cancelled; tool showed a full $1,252.16 refund to original PayPal. For the laptop, agent explained pending order eligibility and got explicit confirmation for both item and tender change. However, the item-modification tool accepted Visa as the tender for the $218.84 price-difference refund but left the original payment record as PayPal; it did not change the order payment method. Agent subsequently disclosed this distinction, checked order details upon follow-up, and correctly said a payment-method change could not be made after the one-time item modification. Caution for similar cases: before committing a one-time item change, clarify whether the requested payment-method change is independently supported and whether the action's payment_method parameter only handles price-difference settlement; don't promise that this updates the order's stored payment tender. Feedback was level none, so no grading judgment is available.

notes.title: Retail order workflow lessons
notes.body: In a retail-agent scenario, authenticate by email or name+ZIP before order access; identify the exact order by inspecting the authenticated customer's orders/status/items. For cancellation, confirm pending status, order ID, and one of the allowed reasons; get explicit yes before cancellation and report refund timing based on original payment method/tool result. For item changes, check pending status and same-product variant availability, collect all requested item changes, price delta, and payment method, then disclose the one-time/irreversible effect and obtain explicit confirmation before the single modification call. Important observed edge case: the item-modification tool accepted a selected card as the method for the price-difference refund but left the original purchase payment method unchanged. Do not claim the order payment method changed unless the resulting order record confirms it. If the customer wants both item and payment-method changes, rules/tool limitations may make sequencing critical: clarify feasibility and preferably perform a separate payment-method change before the one-time item modification, if supported and confirmed; do not assume the item tool will change payment method. Once item modification is performed, this experience reported that no further order modifications/cancellation were possible. Verify state after actions and communicate precisely. No separate evaluation feedback was provided, so do not infer a correctness judgment.

notes.title: Retail case: laptop item modification and payment method
notes.body: In a past retail-agent interaction, the user authenticated with name + ZIP. The assistant identified two orders: pending five-item #W3189752 and pending laptop #W5166363. It obtained explicit confirmation and canceled #W3189752 for “no longer needed”; tool output showed a full $1,252.16 refund on original PayPal method. It identified an available 17-inch i9 laptop variant, item 3265035808, and quoted $2,530.72 versus original $2,749.56. User requested changing items and using Visa for the difference/payment. After confirmation, modify_pending_order_items succeeded, changed the item, and recorded a $218.84 refund to Visa; order remained pending (item modified), with original payment still recorded as PayPal. Assistant correctly reported that the tool result did not change the order payment method and, after rechecking, said the item modification was one-time and no further modification/cancellation was possible. Important ambiguity/possible issue: policy separately allows payment-method modifications on pending orders, but says item modification makes the order no longer modifiable; whether the user could have separately changed payment before item modification was not resolved. The interaction ended by confirming the changed laptop and canceled order; no separate payment-method change occurred. No evaluation feedback was provided, so do not infer grading.

notes.body: From one retail-agent transcript (feedback level reported as “none”; no grading details available): account authentication via name + ZIP located the user, and order lookup correctly identified pending five-item order #W3189752 and pending laptop order #W5166363. Product data showed available matching 100ml variant item 3399869890 at $312.04. After the user explicitly confirmed exchange of all the listed perfume item and refund of the $10.48 difference to original PayPal paypal_6918118, exchange tool returned status 'exchange requested', new item ID 3399869890, and exchange_price_difference -10.48. Agent told user it was requested and mentioned email return instructions. Past task context required valid JSON only, but several assistant replies in the transcript were plain prose, not JSON; this is an observed format mismatch with that stated instruction, without any supplied grading outcome. No separate substantive evaluation feedback was provided (level: none).

notes.title: Retail exchange workflow observations
notes.body: From a retail-agent example (no evaluation feedback provided): The agent authenticated via name + ZIP, retrieved the user/order, then product variants; for a delivered order it matched the requested largest size against the same product options and checked availability. It declined a request to place a new order, which is outside the stated action scope, and offered the supported exchange path. Before exchange it specified all items, target variant, price difference, and refund method, then waited for explicit yes; after tool success it reported the exchange request and return-email instructions. For similar cases: (1) authenticate via permitted identifier before accessing account data; (2) inspect order status/items and product variants; (3) verify same product, option match, target availability and price; (4) explain supported alternatives/limitations; (5) state exact item(s), target, and payment method for any difference, ensuring all desired items are included; (6) stop for explicit confirmation before the single update call; (7) report only what the tool confirms. Unverified caveat: the tool result showed exchange requested and a negative price difference, while the agent described the amount as a refund; do not generalize timing/settlement beyond policy or tool evidence. The supplied task context says outputs must be valid JSON only, but the transcript's customer-facing messages were plain text; compliance with that formatting instruction was therefore not demonstrated. No feedback indicates whether this behavior was graded correct.

notes.title: Retail pending item modification: refund timing wording
notes.body: In a public retail-support interaction, the agent authenticated via name+ZIP, identified a pending order and an available same-product variant matching requested capacity/material/color, disclosed the one-time modification limitation and requested explicit confirmation, then modified only after the user said yes. Tool output showed a refund transaction for the $6.28 price difference to the original Visa. However, the supplied policy says non-gift-card refunds take 5–7 business days, while the final reply said the difference “has been refunded” without timing. In similar cases, distinguish a recorded/initiated refund from funds being received and mention the policy’s 5–7 business-day window; the exact processing semantics were not independently verified here. No separate evaluation feedback was provided.

notes.title: Retail pending-order item modification workflow
notes.body: In the supplied retail-agent experience, the customer was authenticated via name+ZIP, then an order was identified from the authenticated user's listed order IDs and checked for status/items. For a pending item change: inspect product variants, confirm the exact same-product available variant and price/options; disclose any uncertainty (the system could verify listed variant attributes but not whether it matched the customer's separate bottle); collect all items to change and payment method; clearly state one-time/irreversible implications and price difference; obtain explicit yes/no confirmation to the complete action before invoking modification; then report the tool result. In this instance the selected available 1L stainless-steel black variant was $6.28 cheaper, and the tool response showed a refund to the original Visa and pending status with items modified. This is an observed successful tool sequence, not proof that every agent message was policy-perfect. No separate evaluation feedback was provided (level none). For similar work, stop and ask if target variant details or payment method are unresolved; do not claim exact identity beyond known attributes.

notes.title: Retail requests: authenticate, verify, confirm, then act
notes.body: In one retail-support interaction, the user requested a jacket exchange and a default-address update. The agent authenticated by email and checked profile details, then identified the jacket among the user's orders (checking order statuses) and looked up product variants. The jacket order was pending, so the agent clearly explained it would be handled as a pending-item modification rather than a delivered-order exchange; it verified the exact same-product available variant, size, price difference, payment method, and one-time/non-cancellable consequence, and obtained explicit confirmation before modifying. It also presented the complete Washington, DC address found on an order and obtained confirmation before updating the profile default address. Tool results confirmed the item change, refund to PayPal, and address update; the agent reported these outcomes. Procedure for similar work: (1) authenticate using email or name plus ZIP before accessing account data; (2) identify the relevant order/item and inspect its status; (3) inspect product variants and availability if changing an item; (4) branch by status/action eligibility—pending item change is a modification, delivered order may qualify for exchange; do not characterize one as the other; (5) state exact item(s), variant, price difference/payment method, and irreversible/one-time effects as applicable, and collect explicit confirmation before any database update; ensure all intended items are included; (6) for a default-address change, obtain the complete address and explicit confirmation; (7) perform the confirmed update(s), inspect tool result, and report only verified outcomes. This interaction succeeded, but provides no separate evaluation feedback; don't treat it as evidence of universal correctness.

notes.title: Retail order changes and address confirmations
notes.body: In one retail-support interaction, the customer called a requested change an “exchange,” but the jacket order was pending; the agent checked the order and correctly framed it as a pending-order item modification, not a delivered-order exchange. It identified an available same-product option, stated the price difference and payment method, disclosed the one-time/permanent modification consequence, and got explicit confirmation before modifying. The tool result showed a $6.74 PayPal refund, which was reported accurately. The customer also explicitly confirmed a Washington address previously found on one of their orders before the profile default address was updated. Lesson/caution: check order status and distinguish pending modifications from delivered exchanges; verify the exact variant, availability, and price delta, and obtain explicit confirmation for every consequential update (including default-address changes). This lesson applies when handling retail orders under policies that restrict actions by status. No separate evaluation feedback was provided, so the interaction’s correctness is not independently graded.

notes.title: Retail pending-order changes: sequence, confirmation, and variant checks
notes.body: In one retail-agent experience, a user requested both a shipping-address change and item modification on a pending order. Authenticate first via email or name+ZIP, then retrieve the user's orders/details as needed. If the user identifies an address from their other order, verify it belongs to the same authenticated user and read the complete address from that order; confirm the intended address before updating. For product substitutions, inspect product variants, filter to available variants matching requested attributes, then compare prices to find the cheapest qualifying option; keep product ID and item ID distinct. Policy says item modification is one-time and afterward the order cannot be modified or cancelled, so gather all requested item changes and the required payment method, clearly state details/lockout, and obtain explicit yes confirmation before the item-modification call. In the observed case, the agent updated the address first after confirmation, then modified the item after a separate explicit yes, and both tool calls succeeded; the item tool recorded a refund of the price difference to the original PayPal. This is evidence of that sequence succeeding in that case, not a guarantee for all orders. The agent initially warned both might not be possible, but subsequent tool results showed both were completed; do not claim impossibility without checking applicable tool/policy behavior. After each action, verify the returned order state and report only what it establishes. No separate evaluation feedback/details were provided.

notes.title: Retail pending-order modification incident
notes.body: In a retail support interaction, authentication via name+ZIP located the customer despite forgotten email/order ID, then order lookup identified a pending order with two requested item changes and a delivered boots order. Catalog checks found desired variants and prices. Important incident: assistant correctly recognized a pending order can be modified (not exchanged), but called the one-time modify tool before getting explicit confirmation of the exact changes and payment method, contrary to the supplied policy requiring action details and explicit yes. Tool output was inconsistent: it listed the skateboard replacement item ID/options/price for both skateboard and luggage; despite available desired luggage variant being verified earlier, actual luggage update is unverified. A pending-item modification is one-time and locks out further modification/cancellation per policy, so be cautious. Assistant disclosed inconsistency, did not claim verified success, and transferred after user requested human review; transfer succeeded. Hiking boots return was not submitted: no explicit confirmation to action plus refund method was collected. For similar cases, authenticate; identify orders and status; distinguish pending modification from delivered exchange/return; verify each requested variant and availability; list every change, exact payment method and price difference, and confirm all changes with explicit yes before the one-time tool call. After action, inspect tool output item-by-item; if inconsistent, stop and avoid further edits, explain uncertainty and escalate if user asks/cannot resolve. For return, obtain item/order confirmation and refund method before taking action. Feedback provided was level none, so no grading conclusions.

notes.title: Retail service workflow observations
notes.body: For similar retail-support tasks, follow an ordered, checked workflow: (1) authenticate first using email or name + ZIP; don't rely on user ID alone. (2) Once authenticated, inspect listed orders individually when user describes contents rather than knowing order ID; verify owner, exact items, and status, and disclose any additional items relevant to identifying a match. (3) For product changes, fetch variant details and verify same product type, exact requested options, availability, and price difference; explain unavailable options and offer available matches without choosing for the user. (4) Before any database-changing action, summarize exact order/item/address/action, payment method and price difference where relevant, and obtain explicit yes. For once-per-order item modifications/exchanges, explicitly ask whether all desired items have been included; stop if unclear or declined. (5) Make the action call only after confirmation, then report outcome based on tool result, including status, refund/payment direction, and any irreversible limits or return instructions. In the reviewed experience, the address update was confirmed before execution; the pending watch change used an available same-product variant, disclosed its $121.20 refund and irreversible one-time limit, and confirmed completeness; delivered purifier exchange checked availability and $24.24 additional charge and confirmed completeness. Tool result for the exchange recorded 'exchange requested' and exchange fields while the listed original order items remained in the response, so describe it as a request/status rather than asserting fulfillment or shipment. No separate evaluation feedback was provided.

notes.title: Retail order-change workflow lessons
notes.body: For similar retail order-change work, use this ordered procedure, subject to the available tools and policy: (1) Authenticate first by email or name+ZIP; only then retrieve profile/orders. (2) Identify target orders and verify status; for pending item changes retrieve product variants and confirm exact same-product option, availability, price. Keep profile address distinct from order shipping address; do not assume a requested NYC address exists merely because user says it is saved. If the shipping destination is unresolved or user says not to ship to the current address, stop and leave the order untouched; re-check the order address after the customer reports updating profile if tools permit. Do not ask them to disclose an address if they decline; explain only secure alternatives actually supported by tools. (3) Before an item modification, collect every intended item change for that order, explain the one-time/non-reversible consequences described by policy, and identify the payment method the user wants for any price difference/refund; policy requires a provided payment method. Do not infer listed item prices are final order totals or claim no fees absent evidence. (4) Provide a clear action summary (order, item/variant, address if relevant, price difference and payment method) and obtain explicit yes confirmation before each database action. User approval of variant/preferences alone is not transaction confirmation. Separate orders require separate actions and confirmations; can proceed back-to-back only after confirming each, and only if prerequisites are met. (5) Call one tool at a time, verify result, then report accurately. Stop if status, address, variant availability, payment method, or confirmation is missing. In one past trace, no modification occurred; the user repeatedly asked both orders remain untouched while updating profile. The assistant appropriately held, but omitted the required price-difference payment-method prerequisite for the price-drop item changes. No timeline was verifiable from the described order tools.
